topics: 🔗 No Transfer of Sanctity — one may not move an item from one holiness to another
💰 Consecration of Value — but the value may be pledged to the Temple treasury
🙅 Rav Huna Refuted — may an altar animal be linked to a priestly dedication?
📜 'Every Dedicated Item' — Ulla rereads Leviticus 27:28 as a me'ilah verse
⏳ Delay of the Treasurers — a burnt offering pledged for maintenance, by Torah law
⚰️ Standing and Valuation — Rabbi Yoḥanan vs. Reish Lakish on what may be redeemed once dead

overview.title: 📖 Overview: What Two Sanctities Can and Cannot Do to Each Other
overview.subtitle: Temurah 32a–32b
overview.hebrewSource: אַךְ כׇּל חֵרֶם אֲשֶׁר יַחֲרִם אִישׁ לַה׳ מִכׇּל אֲשֶׁר לוֹ… לֹא יִמָּכֵר וְלֹא יִגָּאֵל, כׇּל חֵרֶם קֹדֶשׁ קׇדָשִׁים הוּא לַה׳
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Where the previous mishna listed the differences between altar consecration and Temple-maintenance consecration, this one lists what they share: neither may be shifted from one sanctity to another, though one may pledge an animal's value. Rav Huna builds a rule on Leviticus 27:28 — that an altar animal cannot be linked to a priestly dedication — and the Gemara dismantles it with two baraitot, forcing Ulla to reread the verse entirely. The daf closes on a dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish over which consecrated animals were ever included in 'standing and valuation', and therefore which may still be redeemed once they have died.

slides.title: 🙅 Rav Huna's Rule and Its Conclusive Refutation
slides.subtitle: Can an animal consecrated for the altar also be pledged as a dedication to the priests?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rav Huna: he has done nothing. Leviticus 27:28 — 'every dedicated item is most holy' — implies that only what is already most holy can be so dedicated
2️⃣ Objection from a baraita: it bars linking Temple-maintenance items and priestly dedications to other sanctities — and pointedly omits the altar case, implying that one does take effect
3️⃣ Rav Huna's defense: the tanna listed only cases where both other sanctities fail; the altar case is mixed, so it was left out
4️⃣ Second objection: a baraita says outright that one consecrates an altar animal by value and dedicates it to priests; another says that if he did so, what he did is done
5️⃣ ✅ The refutation of Rav Huna is conclusive (תְּיוּבְתָּא) — an altar animal may be linked to a priestly dedication

callout.label: Why the attempt to save him failed:
callout.text: The mishna's own 'one may consecrate their value and one may dedicate them' was first reread as two ways of saying 'for Temple maintenance' — but the baraita spells out that the second phrase means a dedication to priests.

slides.title: 📜 So What Does 'Every Dedicated Item' Teach?
slides.subtitle: Ulla salvages the verse for a different purpose

lines.speaker: Ulla
lines.text: The verse is not read as Rav Huna read it. 'Every dedicated item is most holy' teaches that one is subject to the laws of me'ilah for a dedication to the priests.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Why is a verse needed? The words 'most holy' are right there, and me'ilah applies to all sanctified items!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: By your reasoning, consider Rabbi Yannai: me'ilah is written explicitly only regarding a burnt offering — 'and sin through error in the holy items of the Lord' (Lev. 5:15).

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: And Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi needed 'all the fat is the Lord's' (Lev. 3:16) to include offerings of lesser sanctity — and a fortiori the most sacred ones.

lines.speaker: Conclusion
lines.text: So even where 'most holy' is written, a separate verse is still required to bring an item under me'ilah. The same holds for priestly dedications.

callout.label: Status of the rule:
callout.text: The requirement to pay the value of an altar animal linked to Temple maintenance is rabbinic; Ulla's verse is only supporting ('asmakhta'). By Torah law nothing more than the treasurers' presence is involved.

slides.title: ⏳ A Burnt Offering Consecrated for Temple Maintenance
slides.subtitle: Ulla: only 'the delay of the treasurers' stands in its way

nodes.content: 🐑 One consecrates his burnt offering for Temple maintenance
📖 By Torah law: a burnt offering cannot be consecrated by value at all — the treasurer is now the owner, and an owner must stand over his offering. That is the whole obstacle.
⚖️ By rabbinic law: a baraita forbids slaughtering it until it is redeemed

columns.label: Proof it is only rabbinic
columns.content: The same baraita adds: if he transgressed and slaughtered it first, what he did is done — impossible if redemption were required by Torah law

columns.label: Proof it is not merely rabbinic
columns.content: The baraita's end: one who benefits misuses on two counts — altar and maintenance — which a rabbinic consecration would not generate

callout.label: Left standing:
callout.text: The two clauses of the baraita pull in opposite directions, which is precisely why the Gemara must distinguish Torah law from rabbinic enactment here.

slides.title: ⚰️ If It Died Before It Was Redeemed
slides.subtitle: 'Standing and valuation' (Lev. 27:11–12) decides whether redemption is still possible

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan on the Rabbis
items: Both altar and maintenance animals were included in standing and valuation
Anything that cannot be stood and valued cannot be redeemed
So if either died — it is buried, not redeemed
This is why R' Shimon had to specify 'for Temple maintenance'

boxes.title: Reish Lakish on the Rabbis
items: Only maintenance animals were included — the verse speaks of them
Difficulty: then R' Shimon's specification is redundant

boxes.title: Both agree on R' Shimon
items: Maintenance animals were not in standing and valuation → if they died, redeemed
Altar animals were → if they died, not redeemed
And all agree: an animal blemished from the outset, consecrated for the altar, is redeemable

callout.label: Reish Lakish's reply:
callout.text: Rabbi Shimon did not know which case the first tanna meant, so he addressed it conditionally — 'if you are speaking of altar animals, then…'. A baraita, however, is taught in line with Rabbi Yoḥanan.

slides.title: 🔍 Reading Leviticus 27:11–12 — Blemished or Non-Kosher?
slides.subtitle: The baraita that supports Rabbi Yoḥanan works out whom the verse addresses
rows: They are redeemed through standing and valuation
A non-kosher animal consecrated for maintenance
It would be redeemed through standing and valuation
Lev. 27:27 already states separately: 'if it be of a non-kosher animal, he shall redeem it according to your valuation'

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: 'Then he shall set the animal before the priest, and the priest shall value it' governs blemished consecrated animals — which is the foundation of the whole standing-and-valuation dispute above.

summary.principle: Sanctity cannot be converted from one type to another, but value can be pledged across them — and whether a dead consecrated animal may still be redeemed turns on whether its category was ever subject to 'standing and valuation'.

flowSteps.content: 📜 Mishna: no altering sanctity from one form to another; but one may consecrate an animal's value and dedicate it
🙅 Rav Huna: an altar animal cannot be linked to a priestly dedication → conclusively refuted by two baraitot
📖 Ulla rereads 'every dedicated item is most holy' as the source for me'ilah on priestly dedications; the value payment is rabbinic

columns.content: ⏳ Burnt offering pledged to maintenance: by Torah law only the treasurers' delay
⚰️ Died unredeemed: R' Yoḥanan bars both, Reish Lakish only maintenance animals

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: what cannot be 'stood before the priest and valued' cannot be redeemed — which is why a dead animal's category decides its fate

quiz.q: What did Rav Huna rule about an animal consecrated for the altar that its owner then pledged as a dedication to the priests?
o: The dedication takes effect and he must pay its value
He has done nothing — the pledge is ineffective
The animal must be buried
The priests may choose whether to accept it
quiz.e: Rav Huna read 'every dedicated item is most holy' (Lev. 27:28) to mean that only what is already most holy can be dedicated. The Gemara ultimately declares this a conclusive refutation.

quiz.q: How does Ulla reinterpret the phrase 'every dedicated item is most holy'?
o: As barring the sale of dedicated property
As teaching that one is liable for me'ilah on a dedication to the priests
As requiring the priests to be from the serving watch
As permitting redemption of blemished animals
quiz.e: Since Rav Huna's reading is refuted, Ulla assigns the phrase a different job. The Gemara defends the need for it by noting that even 'most holy' items required separate verses to bring them under me'ilah.

quiz.q: According to Ulla, what by Torah law prevents a burnt offering consecrated for Temple maintenance from being sacrificed?
o: It must first be redeemed by appraisal
Nothing at all — it may be sacrificed immediately
Only 'the delay of the treasurers', since the treasurer is now the owner who must stand over it
It may never be sacrificed and must be buried
quiz.e: By Torah law a burnt offering cannot be consecrated by value. The rule requiring redemption before slaughter is rabbinic, as shown by the baraita's own concession that if he slaughtered it first, what he did is done.

quiz.q: On Rabbi Yoḥanan's account of the Rabbis, what happens to an animal consecrated for the altar that died before being redeemed?
o: It is redeemed like any other
It is buried without redemption, since it was included in standing and valuation
It is given to the priests
It is redeemed only if it was blemished from the outset
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the Rabbis included both altar and maintenance animals in standing and valuation, and what cannot be stood and valued cannot be redeemed. Reish Lakish limits that to maintenance animals.

quiz.q: Why does the baraita reject reading Leviticus 27:11–12 as referring to a non-kosher animal?
o: Non-kosher animals can never be consecrated
Because Leviticus 27:27 already states separately that a non-kosher animal is redeemed according to valuation
Because the priest may not appraise a non-kosher animal
Because the verse mentions 'an offering unto the Lord'
quiz.e: The later verse already covers non-kosher animals, so the earlier one would be redundant on that reading. It is therefore taken to address blemished consecrated animals.
